extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, SDS preparers, safety professionals, and regulatory compliance personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) governing how chemical identities, exact percentages, and concentration ranges may be claimed as trade secrets on Safety Data Sheets (SDSs), including permitted prescribed ranges, combining rules, emergency disclosure to health care professionals, and compliance dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prescribed concentration ranges when claiming exact concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finalized a requirement to utilize prescribed concentration ranges when a manufacturer, importer, or employer claims the exact concentration as a trade secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prescribed concentration ranges generally align with those used by Health Canada. OSHA concluded that requiring prescribed ranges will provide additional information to workers and downstream users and does not significantly compromise CBI given other protections (e.g., claiming chemical identity as CBI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance to provide narrower ranges fully within prescribed ranges (paragraph (i)(1)(vi))
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added paragraph (i)(1)(vi) to allow the SDS preparer to provide a range narrower than the prescribed ranges, provided the narrower range is fully contained within the bounds of a prescribed range listed in (i)(1)(iv) or fully within the bounds of a combination of ranges allowed by (i)(1)(v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If actual ingredient range is 0.9–2% and prescribed combination would be 0.5–5%, the preparer may disclose 0.5–2%, 0.9–5%, or 0.5–2.5% as long as it is fully within the prescribed range/combination. This change alleviates classification or regulatory triggers that would be inadvertantly caused by using a broader prescribed range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for combining prescribed concentration ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finalized combination rules as proposed (with the added allowance for narrower contained ranges), but rejected allowing combinations among all prescribed ranges that would negate usefulness to workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an exact range falls between prescribed ranges (particularly between 0.1% and 30%), manufacturers may combine two consecutive prescribed ranges between (A) and (G) to represent the concentration. OSHA declined to permit unlimited combination of all ranges and indicated combinations that would create ranges above 30% generally make withholding inappropriate because they would be too wide to be meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must use the narrowest range possible that includes true concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must use the narrowest prescribed range (or combination or permitted narrower range) that includes the true concentration range so workers receive the most precise information possible under prescribed ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explicitly rejects suggestions that would permit use of broader prescribed ranges when a narrower one would suffice; the SDS preparer must choose the narrowest applicable range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must reflect most severe hazard of selected range
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifiers are required to classify a substance according to the most severe hazard category into which the highest point of the selected range falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses stakeholder questions about whether selection of a prescribed range could force classification into additional/higher hazard categories; OSHA confirmed classifiers must reflect the most severe category associated with the selected range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three types of information may be claimed as trade secret
rubrics_metrics.description: Under paragraph (i) there are three types of information that manufacturers can claim as a trade secret: the name of a chemical, the exact percentage of a chemical's concentration in a mixture, and/or a concentration range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the final rule, manufacturers may no longer completely withhold the exact percentage without providing a concentration range in its place (a change from the 2012 HCS). The rule clarifies that chemical identity and exact percentage and/or concentration range may be withheld 'and/or' (i.e., more than one may be claimed).

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS Section 3: indicate when identity or concentration is withheld as trade secret and use consistent identifier
rubrics_metrics.description: The SDS must indicate in Section 3 when the specific chemical identity and/or percentage concentration or concentration range is being withheld as a trade secret; the identifier used in Section 3 should be used consistently throughout the SDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's HCS Compliance Directive specifies that if a trade secret is claimed, the SDS must indicate that identity and/or concentration is claimed as a trade secret in Section 3. The same identifier should be used in Section 8 and elsewhere; when health-effect claims are made in other sections (e.g., Section 11), sufficient identity information must be provided to support assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency disclosure to treating PLHCP
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a treating Physician or other Licensed Health Care Professional (PLHCP) determines that a medical emergency exists and the chemical identity and/or specific percentage concentration of a hazardous chemical is needed for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer must immediately disclose the specific chemical identity or percentage composition of a trade secret chemical to that treating PLHCP, regardless of whether a written statement of need or a confidentiality agreement exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SDS preparer or owner of the trade secret may require a written statement of need and a confidentiality agreement in accordance with paragraphs (i)(3) and (4) as soon as circumstances allow; the confidentiality agreement authorized by paragraph (i)(3)(iv) provides remedies to protect CBI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality agreements and remedies to protect CBI
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA authorizes confidentiality agreements under paragraph (i)(3)(iv) and contemplates that such agreements provide remedies to ensure confidential business information is protected after disclosure to PLHCPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although immediate disclosure to a treating PLHCP is required in emergencies, confidentiality agreements and written statements of need can be obtained as soon as practicable to protect CBI; enforcement remedies backstop misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturers may withhold identity and/or concentration or range (clarification of 'and/or')
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA clarified that both chemical identity and the exact percentage (concentration) or concentration range may be claimed as a trade secret — the language 'and/or' makes clear multiple items can be withheld together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies stakeholder concerns that 'or' might be read to mean only one or the other may be withheld; OSHA revised regulatory text to be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on withholding concentration range when combined result would be too broad (>30%)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA stated that if representing a manufacturer's batch would require a combination of ranges above 30 percent (resulting in an excessively wide range), it would generally be inappropriate for a manufacturer to withhold the concentration range from the SDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such circumstances, manufacturers still have the option of withholding the chemical identity instead to protect trade secret information. OSHA emphasized that very wide combined ranges are unlikely to provide meaningful information to workers and would undermine alignment with Canada's system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of PLHCP in place of 'physician and nurse'
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA added a definition of 'Physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP)' and replaced 'physician and nurse' with 'PLHCP' to align with other OSHA standards and current medical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No commenter objected to this revision; PLHCP is defined by scope of practice (license/registration/certification) sufficient to provide or delegate relevant health care services referenced in paragraph (i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspector training and application limited to trade secret claims
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA expects its inspectors to be adequately trained so that paragraphs (i)(1)(iv)-(v) apply only to concentration ranges withheld as trade secrets, not to actual concentration ranges disclosed in SDSs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA declined to adopt a clarification requested by a commenter because it believes the regulatory text already unambiguously applies only to trade secret claims and that inspectors will be trained accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final compliance dates for implementation (paragraph (j))
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA modified the proposed compliance dates: chemical manufacturers, importers, and distributors evaluating substances must comply within 18 months after the publication date, and those evaluating mixtures must comply within 36 months after the publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA considered stakeholder requests for extensions and staggered tiers; it extended the proposed one- to two-year tier modestly to 18 and 36 months but declined to adopt additional staggered tiers based on supply-chain role. OSHA noted many changes can be integrated into normal SDS/label update cycles, but recognized that some revisions may require major changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with Health Canada prescribed ranges as evidentiary basis
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA based the prescribed ranges largely on those used by Health Canada and relied on the long history (since 1988) of their use in concluding they do not demonstrably compromise CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA observed no real-world examples in the record of CBI compromised by Canada's prescribed ranges; comments supporting alignment (including industry commenters) were cited. This alignment informed OSHA's decision to finalize the prescribed ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement as mechanism to address inappropriate trade secret claims
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA stated that potential misuse or inappropriate claiming of trade secret protections should be addressed through enforcement rather than delaying the finalization of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA declined suggestions to postpone allowing withholding of concentration ranges until misuse was eliminated, indicating enforcement actions are the proper remedy for inappropriate claims.
